According to VI 75, free will <note>original Greek: τὸ αὐτεξούσιον (*to autexousion*)</note> is named as the author of the movement.

A detailed and coherent presentation of the nature and consequences of this movement—the Fall—is then found in the *Letter to Melania* (Frankenberg 613 ff.). Through the Fall—this is also a line of thought already familiar to us—the Mind <note>original Greek: *Nus*</note> has lost the unity of its essence. It has fallen from the essence of the divine Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate, indivisible divine unity</note> and entered the world of "number" (see above): "numbers which entered into the Mind because of the movement" <note>original Greek: ἀριθμοὶ οἳ διὰ τὴν κίνησιν εἰς τὸν νοῦν ὑπεισῆλθον</note> (Frankenberg 617). More precisely, the fragmentation of the human being into Mind, soul, and body is a consequence of the movement (617. 190 b α). Even more characteristic is the sentence (Frankenberg 618): "it happens that because of its free will, having fallen from its first state, it was named 'soul' and, having slipped down again... it was called 'body'" ¹), and so one and the same being is now body, soul, and Mind "through the changes of its own choices" <note>original Greek: διὰ τὰς μεταβολὰς τῶν αὐτοῦ προαιρέσεων</note>. Evagrius thus teaches quite clearly a degradation of the Mind to the soul, and again from the soul to the bodily essence through the Fall ²). In a slightly different way and in strict adherence to Platonic psychology, this is expressed in VI 85 as follows: "If we possess desire and anger in common with the beasts, it is clear that these were not created with us at the beginning of creation, but they crept into the rational soul after the movement" ³).

We effortlessly recognize the world of thought and terminology of Origen here throughout. For Origen, too, the fall of creatures is a movement, even if the specific term seems to be missing: "for the Creator allowed voluntary and free movements to the minds he had established" <note>original Latin: *voluntarios enim et liberos motus a se conditis mentibus creator indulsit*</note> (II 9, 2 p. 165 25). He speaks of "the ambiguous and fragile movements of the soul itself" <note>original Latin: *animae ipsius ambigui fragilesque motus*</note> (I 8, 4. 102, 6). — With him, too, the catchphrase appears that man fell through his "negligence" <note>original Greek: ἀμέλεια (*ameleia*)</note> (see above) ⁴). I further recall that a pair of sayings by Evagrius, whose meaning rests on the terminological distinction between Mind <note>original Greek: *νοῦς*</note> and soul <note>original Greek: *ψυχή*</note>, has proven to be a literal quotation from Origen: "the soul that acts is a lyre... the pure Mind is a psaltery" <note>original Greek: κιθάρα ἐστὶν ψυχὴ πρακτική .... ψαλτήριόν ἐστι νοῦς καθαρός</note> (VI 46. 48 see above p. 291).

He demonstrates here how the soul, the "imaginative and impulsive essence" <note>original Greek: οὐσία φανταστικὴ καὶ ὁρμητική</note>, is common to both humans and animals, how the angels are never called "souls" in Scripture, and how the "soul of God" is only spoken of exceptionally and improperly, while it is with

म० २. अ० १. सू० ३. ॥ Book 2. Chapter 1. Hymn 3. ॥ द्वितीयोऽष्टकः ॥ Second Octave ॥ ४३३ Page 433

## Hymn Text
Night and Dawn, the two who are ancient and exalted, move together like two skilled female weavers. They weave the stretched thread of the sacrifice, creating its beautiful form. They are bountiful and full of water. ॥ ६ ॥

> **Ancient/Exalted; actions/works; eternally; for us; sprinkled/worshipped; Dawn and Night; like two female weavers; praised/rejoicing; thread; stretched; weaving; moving together; of the sacrifice; form/beauty; bountiful; full of water.** ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Exalted** refers to those who are praised by our **actions**, meaning our sacrificial works. They are **eternally** worshipped through continuous songs of praise. Alternatively, the word for eternal refers to their perpetual nature. In this case, **sprinkled** means they are the ones who pour out the fruits of the ritual. **Dawn and Night** are the deities of the day and the night. They are described as being **like two weavers**, meaning they are as skilled as women who weave cloth. They are **praised** as they move past one another in succession. They are **weaving** the **stretched thread**, which represents the various parts of the sacrifice that are spread out over time. They work **moving together** in mutual cooperation to produce the ritual. Why do they weave? To create the **form** or the beauty of the **sacrifice being performed**. This means they cause the parts of the sacrifice to be carried out in the correct order. The sacrifices are spread out across the days and nights. They are **bountiful**, meaning they yield the fruits of the ritual. They are **full of water** because rain is produced by the cycle of day and night. May these two great deities of day and night carry out our sacrifice.

---

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
The two divine invokers, the first and most wise, perform the sacrifice rightly with a sacred song. They have excellent forms. Worshipping the gods according to the seasons, they anoint them at the navel of the earth, upon the three heights. ॥ ७ ॥

> **Two divine; invokers; first; most wise; rightly; they sacrifice; together; with a song; most beautiful; the gods; worshipping; according to the season; together; they anoint; at the navel; of the earth; upon; the heights; three.** ॥ ७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Two divine** refers to the divine Agni who exists in heaven. From that divine fire, two **invokers** are born. They are the ones who call the gods or perform the offerings. They are identified as the two fires: the terrestrial fire on earth and the atmospheric fire in the sky. They are the **first** to be worshipped. They are **most wise**, meaning they are the greatest of the learned. They have **excellent forms**. These two gods, through a **sacred song** or mantra, **sacrifice rightly**, which means they perform the worship perfectly without any defect. They **worship the gods** who are worthy of sacrifice **according to the seasons**, meaning at the specific prescribed times. These two gods—

<note>
- **Dawn and Night** (Uṣāsānaktā): These are personified as twin sisters or two weavers who create the fabric of time and ritual.
- **Day and night**: The commentary links the natural cycle of time to the successful completion of the ritual.
- **Two divine invokers** (Daivyā Hotārā): These represent two forms of the fire god Agni, usually understood as the fire on the altar and the lightning in the clouds.
- **Navel of the earth** (Nābhā Pṛthivyā): This is a technical term for the central sacrificial altar, considered the center of the world.
- **Three heights**: This likely refers to the three levels of the world (earth, atmosphere, and heaven) or three specific locations on the altar.
</note>

<summary>
This page translates verses 6 and 7 of the third hymn in the second book, invoking the personified Night and Dawn and the two divine priestly fires. It explains their roles in maintaining the continuity and beauty of the sacrificial ritual.

We have taken them for lumbar vertebrae: here, then, are three kinds of vertebrae.

3. Besides the vertebrae contained in these two blocks, there is also a considerable number of detached vertebrae or fragments of vertebrae. Among these, there are 5 to 6 that have processes similar to the large vertebrae of the first block, several with 3 processes like those we regarded as lumbar vertebrae, and a much larger number still of oblong vertebrae similar to those of which the large block contains five. These oblong vertebrae form a decreasing series, interrupted here and there because of lost vertebrae, which ends almost in a point. The total sum of all the vertebrae arranged by the central school amounts to more than 80. There are still several in the hands of some private individuals who obtained them from the workers before the acquisition was made by the school. I flatter myself that most of these individuals, at least, will give the vertebrae they possess to the Cabinet <note>referring to a museum or scientific collection</note>. So far, as far as I know, only four teeth have been found, one of which—and the fragments of another—are in the Cabinet. They are hollow up to the point, which is slightly curved. The comparison of these teeth with the superb jaws that are in Paris will alone suffice to prove, contrary to what Citizen <term>Faujas</term> <gloss>Barthélemy Faujas de Saint-Fond, a French geologist</gloss> said in his letter, that the animal in question and the one whose head is in Paris are of different species.

There is a bone in a small block that some regard as a rib and others as a tibia. This is, in general, what is deposited in the Cabinet.

Another block and several detached bones have been found since. In this block, there is a sequence of ten vertebrae, arranged as in the living animal; their height is 16 lines <note>a French unit of measurement, approximately 36 millimeters</note>, that of each of the vertebrae of our large block. Their <term>apophyses épineuses</term> <gloss>spinous processes</gloss> are also wider and six inches long. Beside these vertebrae, one sees the impressions of 9 ribs, and part of a rib 8 to 9 inches long. I was very sorry to see that this block had been sawed at the place of the ribs and that no rib has been preserved whole; but the workers say that this was impossible for them given the state of consumption in which the ribs are found due to the infiltration of

<column-break/>

waters that occurred in that place. They say that these ribs were more than three feet long and that they broke into pieces as soon as they touched them, which seems credible, for I have found detached bones that were entirely friable. The piece of rib that is found in the block is almost round, very slightly flattened, and has a curvature. Among the bones that are still drying, there are five or six vertebrae quite different from those that are in the Cabinet. They appear to have been the vertebrae of the neck. The spinous process is well pronounced, and the transverse processes are of a different form from those of the vertebrae that we took for lumbar. In one, the transverse processes are terminated by an uneven convex surface. Among the bones and their debris, there are also some vertebrae with three processes similar to those we called lumbar. There are also two fragments that appear to be parts of two <term>Omoplates</term> <gloss>shoulder blades/scapulae</gloss>.

V.

The truth is that the intent of "statement" is the intellectual meaning.

...one of them, it would not lead to a syllogism. Every statement that is such is not a syllogism. This is how the Sheikh <note>Avicenna</note> mentioned it in *The Healing* <term>al-Shifāʾ</term>. 

It has been said that if this were not considered, it would necessitate that any two propositions would be a syllogism, however they were, because they would necessitate one of them <gloss>meaning they are identical</gloss>. But the necessity of the whole for the part is prohibited, because the meaning of "necessitating from them" is that each one of them must have a role in achieving that result, and neither of them has a role in achieving the other. 

If it is said: This definition applies to the composite proposition that necessitates its converse and its contrapositive, yet it is not called a syllogism. The answer is that these are not "statements" <note>plural</note>, but rather a single statement, so the definition does not apply to it. 

The investigation shows that the intent of his saying "**necessitate by their very essence another statement**" is that those statements must lead to the result by way of logical inquiry <term>al-naẓar</term>. This inquiry is understood because that which leads to a goal by way of inquiry is not a mere accident. How could it not be considered when the purpose of this art <note>logic</note> is to explain the methods of acquiring concepts and assents? Thus, the assent to one of the parts of a composite proposition, even if it necessitates its converse or contrapositive, is not reached by way of logical inquiry.

<margin>
Its being universal requires that it does not exclude other statements that lead to the objective. This requires the correctness of the technical term since they were in a state of leading by way of inquiry, not essentially. The contrapositive is not like that; rather, it holds true as long as the indication is not like the complete one.
</margin>

# The Names of Its Harbors

<margin>
**Harbor descriptions in the outer compartments (starting top left, clockwise):**

1. The Western Tabyun Harbor: protected from the East wind <note>original: "al-Auri"; from the Greek "Euros"</note> and the South wind <note>original: "al-Natus"; from the Greek "Notus"</note>. 2. Butis Harbor: protected from the "Head" wind <note>likely a local nautical term for a wind coming from a specific headland</note>. 3. Qablasi Harbor: suitable for a single ship. 4. Fadlah Harbor: for a ship, protected from the South wind and other winds. 5. Harbor of the Seven Springs. 6. Harbor of Wadi Lid: protected from the North wind <note>original: "al-Bulus"; from the Greek "Boreas"</note>. Harbor of the Fortress: protected from the Head wind and the "Bear" wind <note>original: "al-Dub"; likely referring to a North wind associated with the Great Bear constellation</note>; it guards the village. 3. Salwah Harbor: protected from the South wind, used by large merchant ships. 4. Latiyah Harbor: large, protected from the Butis and Frankish winds, and a large valley. 5.
